cues.en: Welcome to the last week in the Theory and Practice of Cryptography course, and it's my pleasure to welcome Ben Adida to give the final talk on cryptographic voting protocols and verifying elections with cryptography. Ben is currently on the research faculty at Harvard Medical School working on some privacy aspects of electronic medical records and has done a lot of work with voting in the past and is also
cues.zh: 欢迎来到“密码学理论与实践”课程的最后一周，我非常荣幸地邀请到 Ben Adida 来做最后一场演讲，主题是密码学投票协议以及如何用密码学验证选举。Ben 目前在哈佛医学院担任研究教员，主要研究电子病历的隐私保护，他过去在投票系统方面做过大量工作，同时也是

cues.en: on the research group at Harvard. And so without any further ado, I'd like to turn it over to Ben. Hi, everyone. Last year at this time, almost exactly at this time, I gave a talk on voting. If you were at that talk, don't worry. You'll get new information at this talk. If you were not at that talk, don't worry either. I'll go over some of the basic stuff I went over back then. But this talk should be more technical. You guys have had a little bit of crypto with Steve.
cues.zh: 哈佛大学该研究小组的成员。那么闲话少说，下面把时间交给 Ben。大家好。去年的这个时候，几乎就是同一天，我也做过一次关于投票的演讲。如果你当时听过，别担心，今天这场会有新的内容。如果你没听过，也不用担心，我会回顾一下当时讲过的一些基础知识。不过这次演讲会更偏技术性一些，毕竟你们已经跟 Steve 学过一点密码学了。

cues.en: So we'll get into some details of cryptographic voting protocols. And I'm going to try to keep the beginning of it high level, very sort of general protocols, and dig into the crypto about halfway through, approximately. So please interrupt me at any time with questions. I prefer them when you think of them, as opposed to at the end. So raise your hand. And Steve, you'll let me know if somebody asks online. So please don't hesitate to.
cues.zh: 接下来我们会深入探讨密码学投票协议的一些细节。前半部分我会尽量讲得概括一些，介绍一些通用协议，大概讲到一半的时候再深入探讨密码学本身。所以大家有任何问题都可以随时打断我。我更希望大家想到了就问，而不是留到最后。随时举手就好。另外 Steve，如果线上有人提问，麻烦你提醒我一下。所以大家千万别客气。

cues.en: I am, Steve, or whatever you do to ask a question over the network. So as Steve said, right now I'm a research faculty at the Harvard Medical School where I think about privacy of health records. But for my entire PhD and for a chunk of my time right now, I think about what cryptography can bring to the field of elections, in the sense that elections, well, there's issues around elections.
cues.zh: 发私信给 Steve，或者用网上的任何方式提问都行。正如 Steve 所说，我目前在哈佛医学院担任研究员，主要研究健康档案的隐私问题。不过在攻读博士的整个期间，包括现在的很大一部分时间，我都在思考密码学能给选举领域带来什么，毕竟选举嘛，确实存在不少问题。

cues.en: Last year, there were a whole bunch of articles published right around election time. And the articles went something like this. Does e-voting need paper trails? There was one state sued over the lack of paper trail. Actually, more than one state sued in that situation. There was an HBO documentary which came out really right around election time that said, basically, your vote's not going to count. It's going to be trashed. You might as well not vote. In California,
cues.zh: 去年大选期间，一下子冒出了大量的报道，内容大致是这样的：电子投票需要纸质存根吗？有一个州因为缺少纸质存根被起诉了，实际上，因为这事被起诉的还不止一个州；HBO在临近大选时推出了一部纪录片，基本上就是说，你的投票根本不会作数，直接会被扔进垃圾桶，你还不如别去投了；而在加州，

cues.en: There was a report that said that the voting machines there were letting people vote more than once. And in basically three days before the election, there was a report that said Hugo Chavez is in your voting machine. And the headline was justified because a board member of one of the voting machine companies turned out to be from Venezuela and had some prior business associations with Hugo Chavez. Thus, Hugo Chavez is in your voting machine.
cues.zh: 有报道称当地的投票机允许人们重复投票；甚至在大选前三天，还有报道宣称“Hugo Chavez 潜入了你的投票机”；这个抓人眼球的标题之所以能成立，是因为其中一家投票机公司的董事会成员恰好来自委内瑞拉，而且之前还和 Hugo Chavez 有过商业往来，于是就得出了“Hugo Chavez 潜入了你的投票机”的结论。

cues.en: So on the one hand, you had all these articles that said, we're in trouble. You might as well not vote, or vote by mail, or vote on paper. Whatever you can do, just find a piece of paper and write your vote on it. And on the other hand, you had the head of the Election Assistance Commission, Paul de Gregorio. The Election Assistance Commission is a federal organization created after the Florida 2000 election fiasco.
cues.zh: 所以一方面，有那么多文章说，我们麻烦大了。你不如别投票，或者邮寄投票，或者用纸投票。不管能做什么，找张纸把你的票写上去就行。另一方面，还有选举协助委员会主席 Paul de Gregorio。选举协助委员会是2000年佛罗里达选举闹剧后成立的联邦机构。

cues.en: that said, OK, we're going to fix this. And Paul de Gregorio wrote an editorial on October 26, 2006, and said, don't worry. Everything's cool. Your vote's going to count. And the thing I want you to notice here is that you have these extreme statements. On the one hand, your vote's not going to count. On the other hand, your vote is definitely going to count. And on both sides, you have no real evidence one way or the other.
cues.zh: 话虽如此，好吧，我们会解决这个问题。Paul de Gregorio 在2006年10月26日写了一篇评论文章，说别担心。一切都没问题。你的选票会算数的。我想让你注意的是，这里有这些极端的说法。一方面，你的票不会被算数。另一方面，你的票肯定会被算数。可两边其实都没有任何真凭实据。

cues.en: because we have very little information as to whether the elections are going well. We have very little information because the process of elections is such that we end up with very little information about whether they were successful. And this talk is going to be about how we can use techniques from cryptography to give us a lot more auditability than you would think is even possible in the case of an election.
cues.zh: 因为关于选举是否顺利进行，我们掌握的信息少之又少。我们知之甚少，是因为选举的整个流程导致我们最终几乎无法获知它是否成功。而今天的演讲将探讨我们如何利用密码学技术，为选举带来远超你想象的可审计性。

cues.en: Of course, things do go bad sometimes. And I can't have an election talk without talking about some of the funny times when they go bad. Here's one quote right after the election. In Roger's precinct, there was more than 100% voter turnout. That's even better than Russia. It's shocking. Better than 100%. In another case, a thief grabbed a voting machine from an election official's car. Now you have to ask yourself, what was the voting machine doing in the election official's car to begin with?
cues.zh: 当然，有时事情确实会搞砸。既然聊到选举，就不得不提一些让人啼笑皆非的翻车现场。这是一篇选举刚结束后的报道：“在罗杰所在的选区，选民投票率超过了100%。”这简直比俄罗斯还厉害。太惊人了，居然超过了100%。另一个案例是，一个小偷从选举官员的车里偷走了一台投票机。这时候你难免会纳闷：投票机一开始究竟为什么会放在选举官员的车里？

cues.en: Well, you have to understand that to get all these voting machines at 5 a.m. in every voting location, the only practical way to do so in some cases is to have the election officials pick them up the night before and drive them in the morning of the elections. So there's all sorts of subtle process issues around actually running an election which make it particularly hard and which lead to such silly headlines. And then, of course, people got really upset.
cues.zh: 你得明白，要让所有投票机在凌晨5点前送到每个投票站，有些情况下唯一可行的办法，就是让选举工作人员前一晚先把机器取走，选举当天早上再开车运过去。所以，实际操办选举会涉及各种微妙的流程问题，这让事情特别难办，也导致了那些荒唐的新闻标题。然后，人们当然就非常不满了。

cues.en: And then one voter smashed a touchscreen machine in Allentown, Pennsylvania. Now, you read that headline, you think maybe the press is just exaggerating. Turns out they're not. They really did smash that voting machine in Allentown, Pennsylvania. And of course, we're gearing up for another election season. So this is all stuff that I talked about last year. But we have new issues coming up.
cues.zh: 然后，一名选民在宾夕法尼亚州阿伦敦砸坏了一台触摸屏投票机。你看到这个标题，会以为也许是媒体在夸大。结果并非如此。他们真的在宾夕法尼亚州阿伦敦砸坏了那台投票机。当然，我们又在为另一个选举季做准备。这些全是我去年讲过的东西。但我们现在又面临新的问题。

cues.en: Right now, in Colorado, the state has just disallowed a whole bunch of voting machines, including touch screens, optical scans, and the statement they've made is a very strong one. They've said, the standards for evaluating voting machines at the federal level, the federal level standards, are no good. We cannot trust the federal standards. We're going to have our own standards for evaluating voting machines. It's a pretty strong statement, you know, as far as election official statements go.
cues.zh: 眼下，科罗拉多州刚刚禁用了大批投票机，包括触摸屏和光学扫描设备，而且他们发表的声明语气非常强硬。他们表示，联邦层面评估投票机的标准根本不行。我们不能信任联邦标准。我们将制定自己的投票机评估标准。就选举官员的表态而言，这可以说是非常强硬的声明了。

cues.en: And this might trigger a few other states to do the same thing. In Ohio, there was a security review that was just published last week about some of the voting machines they use there. And they found out that using a PDA with the infrared port and a magnet to dislodge something inside the voting machine, they're able to basically completely override the software that runs the voting machine and therefore completely corrupt whatever that voting machine is doing.
cues.zh: 这可能会引发其他几个州效仿。俄亥俄州上周刚发布了一份安全审查报告，针对的是他们那里使用的一些投票机。他们发现，利用带有红外接口的 PDA，再加上一块用来移开投票机内部部件的磁铁，基本上就能完全覆盖运行投票机的软件，从而彻底篡改该投票机正在进行的任何操作。

cues.en: So things are pretty bad in terms of voting machine equipment, in terms of the process. But they're very bad because it's quite hard. Now I'm going to tell you a little bit about why it's hard. This is an excerpt from a story that I also showed this last year. And I really love showing this because it represents one of the core issues of designing cryptographic protocols, or secure protocols in general. Here's a story about a guy who was running for an election.
cues.zh: 投票机设备、整个流程，情况都相当糟。但之所以这么糟，是因为这非常难。现在我要稍微讲讲为什么难。这是我去年也展示过的一个故事片段。我很喜欢展示它，因为它体现了设计密码协议——或者说广义上的安全协议——的核心问题之一。下面讲一个家伙竞选的故事。

cues.en: And his wife, in a tiny, tiny locality, and his wife Roxanne goes to City Hall to see the election results, and he got zero votes. So she comes home to him and says, hey, did you vote for yourself? Because if you did, then something's wrong with the election. And if you didn't, then why didn't you? But what's funny about this is not so much that there were zero votes for him. It's that his wife came home to ask him if he'd voted for himself.
cues.zh: 在一个极小极小的地方，他的妻子 Roxanne 去市政厅看选举结果，结果他得了零票。于是她回家问他：嘿，你投给自己了吗？因为如果你投了，那选举就有问题；如果你没投，那你为什么不投？但好笑的地方倒不是他得了零票，而是他妻子回家来问他有没有投给自己。

cues.en: What this means is she clearly didn't vote for him, right? If she'd voted for him, she wouldn't need to ask him this question, right? And the reason I point this out is because there are inherent limits to what you can do with certain protocols. The security can only be so good. If you get zero votes, it doesn't matter how secure the process is, you know your wife didn't vote for you, right? It doesn't matter how good the rest of the protocol is. So it's interesting when you design security protocols to look at the inputs and outputs and figure out
cues.zh: 这意味着她显然没有投给他，对吧？要是她投了，根本就不需要问他这个问题，对吧？我指出这一点的原因是，某些协议能做到的事情是有其内在局限的。安全性只能做到这种程度。如果你得了零票，过程再安全也没用，你知道你妻子没投你，对吧？协议的其他部分再好也没意义。所以设计安全协议时，观察输入和输出并弄清楚

cues.en: what the best case scenario is. And in the voting case, there are limits to what you can do. Here's a little bit of history, some of you might know it, about how we got here in the first place. And it helps to explain things a little bit. In the beginning of mechanization of voting machines in the 1920s and 30s approximately, we had these lever machines that came out. And these machines basically had counters, and you turn these little levers, and if you lived in New York in the past
cues.zh: 最好的情况会是怎样，这很有意思。而在投票这个场景中，你能做的是有限的。这里有一点历史背景，你们中有些人可能知道，讲的是我们最初是如何走到这一步的。这有助于做一点解释。在大约1920和1930年代投票机机械化之初，出现了这种杠杆式投票机。这些机器基本上装有计数器，你扳动这些小杠杆，如果你过去几年

cues.en: few years, you've seen them in use. They're still in use in some places. I don't know what the status is for 2008. They're supposed to be phasing them out, but you never know. So you turn some levers next to the names you want, and there are some fancy hardware interlocks that prevent you from voting for two different candidates in the same race. And then you pull this big lever, and kachink, all the levers reset, your vote is counted. Don't worry, everything is cool. You can leave the voting booth now.
cues.zh: 住在纽约，你就会见过它们在使用。在某些地方它们现在仍在使用。我不知道2008年它们的情况如何。它们本该被逐步淘汰，但谁知道呢。所以你扳动你想选的名字旁边的杠杆，还有一些精巧的硬件联动装置防止你在同一场竞选中选两个不同的候选人。然后你拉动这个大杠杆，“咔嚓”一声，所有的杠杆都复位了，你的票被计入了。别担心，一切搞定。你现在可以离开投票间了。

cues.en: In fact, they had set them up so that when you pull the lever, it also opened the curtain at the same time. It's very convenient. So these machines may have issues. In particular, they only keep an aggregate count of the ballots. And they're mechanical. So they have mechanical failures. And so there was a statistical analysis done on results based on elections that were run with this kind of equipment. And it turns out that the Digit 9 appears a lot more often in these election results than it
cues.zh: 事实上，他们把机器设置成：你一拉杆，它也会同时拉开帘子。这很方便。所以这些机器可能有问题。尤其是，它们只保存选票的总计数。而且它们是机械的，所以会有机械故障。于是有人对使用这类设备进行的选举结果做了统计分析。结果发现，数字 9 在这些选举结果中出现的频率，远高于它

cues.en: should randomly. And the reason for that is that these counters tend to get stuck when they turn. And when they get stuck, they usually get stuck rolling over between 9 and 0. So when you vote and you're at 9, your vote might not get counted. It might not trigger the thing to roll over. In the 50s and 60s, we decided, OK, well, these punch cards that we're using for computers, they could be useful for tabulating votes too. And in fact, it was actually quite a good idea.
cues.zh: 随机情况下应有的水平。原因在于，这些计数器转动时容易卡住。而一旦卡住，通常是在从 9 翻到 0 的时候卡住。所以当你投票时，如果计数正停在 9，你的一票可能不会被计入，可能触发不了它翻过去。到了 50 年代和 60 年代，我们决定：好吧，我们给计算机用的这些打孔卡，也许也能用来统计选票。事实上，这还真是个相当不错的主意。

cues.en: Because if a punch card system works well, you have a record of every ballot. One ballot is one card. And if everything goes smoothly, you can do recounts. You can inspect them and try to see which holes have been punched and such. But of course, we know the story with what happens when the equipment gets old and when people don't punch holes all the way. And butterfly ballots make people vote for the wrong candidate, potentially. It can get messy.
cues.zh: 因为如果打孔卡系统运转良好，你就能留下每张选票的记录。一张选票就是一张卡片。要是进展顺利，你还可以重新计票。你可以逐张检查，看看打穿了哪些孔等等。但我们当然也清楚后来的故事，一旦设备老化、人们没把孔完全打穿，就会出状况。而且“蝴蝶选票”还可能导致选民投错候选人。局面会变得一团糟。

cues.en: in part because the layout of the ballots was made to fit these punch cards. And so the weird butterfly design, if you've ever seen the Florida 2000 ballot, where you have candidates on the left and on the right and arrows pointing from both sides, then it's kind of hard to align which one is which. That is because of the constraints of punch cards with these holes that are close together. And so you're trying to maximize how much data you can fit.
cues.zh: 部分原因在于，选票的排版正是为了迁就这些打孔卡。如果你见过2000年佛罗里达州的选票，就会发现那种奇怪的蝴蝶式设计：候选人分列左右两侧，两边都有箭头指向中间，这让人很难对齐谁是谁。这正是由于打孔卡上孔位紧挨着的物理限制造成的。所以当时的做法，就是在竭力塞进尽可能多的数据。

cues.en: on one of these punch cards. The principle was a good idea. Fitting the user interface to the technology turns out to have pretty disastrous effects when the race is close. Then eventually we started moving to optical scanners. At first the scanners were centrally located, meaning you filled out your ballot and then you just dropped it in a box and eventually they were moved to a central location and scanned there. The problem with that is that if there's a mistake on your ballot, you filled in too many bubbles, you don't get any feedback right away.
cues.zh: 就在这样一张打孔卡上。这个原则本身是个好主意。让用户界面去迁就技术，结果在选情胶着时造成了相当灾难性的后果。后来我们最终开始转向光学扫描仪。起初扫描仪集中放置在中心地点，也就是说，你填好选票，把它投进箱子里，最后选票会被运到中心地点再扫描。问题在于，如果你的选票出错，比如涂了太多气泡，你不会立刻得到任何反馈。

cues.en: In fact, the only time we know that you filled in too many bubbles for one candidate is when it's too late. At the central location, when we count your ballot, it's a bad ballot. Oh, well. There's no way to reach the voter again. So we moved to precinct-based optical scan, where if you vote in Massachusetts, you've seen these, and they're kind of all over the place now. There's about 40% to 50% of voting machines that work like this. You fill in some bubbles. You feed in the paper. It gets scanned. If there's an error, it gets spit out.
cues.zh: 事实上，我们唯一能知道你给某位候选人涂了太多气泡的时候，已经太晚了。在中心地点计票时，才发现你的选票是废票。唉，算了。已经没办法再联系到这位选民了。于是我们转向基于选区的光学扫描；如果你在马萨诸塞州投票，你见过这些设备，现在它们已经相当普及了。大约 40% 到 50% 的投票机是这样工作的。你涂几个气泡，把纸送进去，它就会被扫描。如果有错误，它会被吐出来。

cues.en: And you're told there's an error, and you get a chance to revoke. And then, of course, there's the touchscreen machines. The main advantage that touchscreen machines have over optical scan is in places where there's a whole bunch of different languages. In LA County, you need to support 16 different languages. And having 16 different pre-printed optical scan ballots, 16 different types of pre-printed ballots, is very painful. So there's a good reason for all of these technical progressions, but security was never
cues.zh: 系统会提示出错，你还有机会撤销。当然，接着就出现了触摸屏机器。相比光学扫描，触摸屏机器的主要优势体现在需要支持多种不同语言的地区。在洛杉矶县，你得支持 16 种不同的语言。而要准备 16 种预印好的光学扫描选票，也就是 16 种不同类型的预印选票，处理起来非常痛苦。所以所有这些技术演进都有充分的理由，但安全性从来都不是

cues.en: the major issue. And if you talk to election officials, you find out that really they care about people participating in the election first. That's the major issue that they try to solve. And then security effectively becomes second. Any questions so far? Is that? Yeah? All right. I'm trying to, yeah. Did DEVIL change its name? Yeah. They just changed their name to Premier Election Systems. Not the whole company, just the election department. Yeah.
cues.zh: 首要考虑的问题。如果你去和选举官员聊聊，就会发现他们最关心的其实是让大家参与到选举中来。这才是他们努力去解决的核心问题。而安全性实际上就退居其次了。到目前为止有什么问题吗？那个？有吗？好的。我想确认下，对。DEVIL 改名了吗？是的。他们刚改名为 Premier Election Systems。不是整个公司，只是选举部门改了。是的。

cues.en: Any other questions? To be extra fair, I think Diebold gets a lot of the wrap. But really, none of the vendors have done that much in that regard. They've tried in very good faith to make elections easier. But the problem is that we have no evidence that things are working well. And so they could be working poorly. Do the touchscreen-based solution produce paper? Some of them have been adapted to produce paper trails. The machines that are adapted to produce paper trails

cues.zh: 或是她的狗受到威胁，她心想“我爱我的狗，不能没有它，为了狗我宁愿被胁迫”。即便在这种情况下，我们也要杜绝这种可能。所以这不仅是自愿的投票隐私，而是强制的无记名投票。我们过去并不总是这样。这其实是个相当现代的概念。这是美国早期选举时的投票方式。看这个穿红衣服的人当着全场观众投票，把选票交给了正在为他主持宣誓的穿蓝衣服的人。

cues.zh: 是的。对。这个问题我之前有点搁置了，不然要回答的东西太多了。问题是最后谁来解密计票结果？解密是由若干选举官员一起通过门限方案完成的，也就是说，只有他们全都到场，比如每个党派一名代表，才能执行最后一步解密。这样就能防止任何单一党派解密单个密文。

But the fact that it's there on the ballot can prevent some of the ugliness from happening at the registration of candidates, at the time of registration of candidates, right? There's this sort of disincentive to make it too hard to register as a candidate because you could always run a write-in campaign. Who knows if it really works in that sense, but it's there. And it's one of the attributes that we would have to preserve.
cues.zh: 当然，并不是每个人都会这么做。自主另选候选人是个挺特别的问题，大家都知道，这类候选人极少能胜出。但选票上有这个选项，就能在候选人登记阶段遏制一些丑陋的勾当，对吧？它能在一定程度上打消把候选人登记门槛设得过高的念头，因为人们总能发起另选候选人竞选。天知道这在实际中到底管不管用，但它确实存在。这也是我们必须保留的特性之一，

cues.en: if we wanted this to be a real system. And there's another issue, which is that sometimes people don't feel so good about the idea that individual ballots go poof, right? The idea that you only get the aggregate at the end of the day, sometimes people aren't very comfortable with that. They want the individual ballots to remain. So there are solutions, fantastic solutions to being able to anonymize individual ballots instead of using this homomorphic combination to whittle them down to one ciphertext.
cues.zh: 如果我们想把它做成一个真正的系统的话。此外还有另一个问题，那就是有时人们对于单张选票直接“凭空消失”的做法感到不太踏实，对吧？最终只能拿到汇总结果，大家有时对此不太放心。他们希望单张选票能够保留下来。所以有一些方案，非常出色的方案，能够将每张单独的选票匿名化，而不是用同态合并将它们缩减为单一的密文。

cues.en: And the class of protocols that does this is called mix nets. You may have heard of mix nets in anonymous communication protocols. There are different kinds of mix nets. The ones we use in voting are called robust mix nets, or sometimes synchronous mix nets, or basically they do all their mixing in huge batches. They don't mix in small batches like various anonymous email protocols do. This is about.
cues.zh: 实现这种机制的一类协议叫作混淆网络（mix nets）。你可能在匿名通信协议中听说过混淆网络。混淆网络有很多种。我们在电子投票中使用的是鲁棒混淆网络（robust mix nets），有时也叫同步混淆网络，基本上它们所有的混合都是大批量进行的。它们不会像各类匿名电子邮件协议那样小批量混合。这种做法在于……

cues.en: waiting for all the inputs and then producing a mixed batch of the inputs. And the idea is that a mixed net is composed of a number of mixed servers run by mutually distrusting parties. So think of it as there's a ballot box of votes, and the Republicans are going to shake it up, and the Democrats are going to shake up the ballot box, and the independents are going to shake up the ballot box. And because everybody's had a turn, everybody can trust that they've shaken it up enough that
cues.zh: 等待所有输入到位，然后生成一批混合后的输入。它的核心思想是，混淆网络由互不信任的多方运行的若干混淆服务器组成。可以把它想象成一个装满选票的票箱，共和党人摇一摇，民主党人也摇一摇，独立人士也来摇一摇。正因为每个人都参与摇过了，大家就能确信票箱已经被充分摇匀，以至于……

cues.en: Nobody knows which vote went where. And literally, the idea is to take every individual input and encrypted vote, shuffle them, and output them. The problem is when you're dealing with data and cipher texts that are unique because we said we use randomization so that no two encrypted ballots for Obama ever look the same. Well, if I just take a whole bunch of data and shuffle them,
cues.zh: 谁也不知道哪张票最终去了哪里。字面意思上，它的思路就是接收每一份单独的输入和加密选票，将它们打乱，然后输出。问题在于，当你处理的是独一无二的数据和密文时——因为我们说过要使用随机化，确保投给 Obama 的两张加密选票看起来绝不相同。那么，如果我只是拿来一大堆数据直接打乱，

cues.en: It's not really hard to figure out where they came from, right? They're unique values. They're just bits. How do we actually shuffle them? So we actually need to modify the values along the way. And the simplest way to do that is using something called a chow mein mixnet or an onion. And that is to say the value that goes in is not just the encryption of a message. It's the layered encryption of the message.
cues.zh: 其实不难推断出它们来自哪里，对吧？它们是唯一的值，只是一串比特位。那我们到底该怎么打乱它们呢？所以我们需要在传输过程中修改这些值。最简单的方法是使用一种叫做 Chaumian 混淆网（mixnet）或洋葱路由的技术。也就是说，输入的数值不仅仅是一条消息的加密，而是消息的分层加密。

cues.en: First, the message is encrypted with the last mixed server's public key, and then with the middle mixed server's public key, and then with the first mixed server's public key. So it's like an onion with layers of encryption. And it hopefully doesn't make you cry. But the message goes through the first server, and it gets decrypted. One layer gets decrypted. The mixed server can't go any further. It can only do that one layer, because only it has that secret key, and it doesn't have the secret keys for the internal layers.
cues.zh: 首先，消息用最后一个混淆服务器的公钥加密，接着用中间混淆服务器的公钥加密，然后再用第一个混淆服务器的公钥加密。所以它就像一颗层层加密的洋葱。希望这不会把你辣哭。随后消息经过第一个服务器并被解密，解开了一层。混淆服务器无法继续解密，它只能解开这一层，因为只有它拥有对应的私钥，并没有内层所需的私钥。

cues.en: So one layer gets undone, and then it gets shifted to a new position, and there you go. So the outputs don't look anything like the inputs. And the same thing for the second mix server. It unwraps one layer, shifts it to a different position. And the same thing for the third one, and at the end, poof, out comes the plain text vote, and we can all count them. Does that make sense? Is there a problem with the system? Exactly, right? I mean, the mix server can do whatever it wants, right? It could, at this point,
cues.zh: 解开一层，换到一个新位置，这就成了。所以输出和输入看起来完全不同。第二台混洗服务器也是同样的操作。它解开一层，移到一个不同的位置。第三台也一样，最后，“嘭”的一声，明文选票就出来了，我们就可以统计了。明白了吗？这个系统有什么问题吗？没错，对吧？我是说，混洗服务器可以为所欲为，对吧？在这个阶段，它完全可以——

cues.en: It could just produce a value that is the double-layered encryption of whatever plain text it wants. So how do we trust? We can trust this for privacy, the fact that enough shuffling is happening. But we can't trust this for integrity, because the MixNet could introduce any values it wants. So protocols that verify MixNets, there's tons of them. And they're fascinating. And there's so much cool math there. But the simplest one, the most beautiful one, involves very little math. And it's a protocol that's due.
cues.zh: 它完全可以随意生成一个明文的双层加密值。那我们该怎么信任它呢？在隐私方面我们能信任它，因为确实做了足够的混洗洗牌。但在完整性方面我们无法信任，因为 MixNet 可以随意引入任何它想要的值。验证 MixNet 的协议有很多很多。它们非常迷人，蕴含了许多酷炫的数学。但最简单、最优雅的一个，几乎用不到什么数学。这个协议出自——

cues.en: to Jacobson, Jewels, and Rivest, and it's from 2002, and it goes something like this. Well, if a mix server has mixed a bunch of votes, let's audit it by asking how it mixed half of them. So where did you mix this one? I mixed it here, and here's the proof of how I decrypted it. The mix server has to reveal that information. What about this one, and this one, and this one, and this one? OK.
cues.zh: 由 Jacobson、Jewels 和 Rivest 在 2002 年提出，大概是这样的。如果一个混淆服务器混合了一批选票，我们可以通过询问它是如何混合其中一半来审计它。“那么这张选票你混到哪去了？”“我混到这儿了，这是我如何解密它的证明。”混淆服务器必须公开这些信息。“那这张呢？还有这张？这张？还有这张呢？”好的。

cues.en: I've audited half of them. And then when we ask the next mixed server, well, we're careful to ask about different ones, so we don't create a whole path all the way through. cues.zh: 而白盒测试中，你甚至能拿到源代码和算法。是否有理由认为，整个过程中的一切都应该可验证，一直细化到底层的二进制代码？不仅是验证结果，还包括输入的源代码。问得非常好。问题在于，这是黑盒测试与白盒测试的对比。我们是否也应该去验证其中的算法以及内部的一切？我认为，是的，如果所有代码都能摆在那里供你验证，那当然很好。

cues.en: But the problem is that you have no idea which code is actually running on the machine. So the only thing you can do is black box testing. And the only thing you can do is verify that the results, not the process, was done correctly. And this is actually a really interesting distinction that at first sounds very subtle. But actually, it's very key to this whole thing, which is that.
cues.zh: 但问题在于，你根本无从得知机器上实际运行的是哪段代码。所以你唯一能做的就是黑盒测试。你唯一能做的，就是验证结果是否正确，而不是过程。这实际上是一个非常有趣的差异，起初听起来很微妙。但实际上，它对整件事来说至关重要，那就是。

cues.en: We give up on verifying that the source code has been correctly installed. We give up on verifying even that the source code is correct. We only check the results and the mathematical proofs of the result. So it's a black box proof that gives you exactly what you need, which is to say these cipher texts were correctly mixed. That's all you care about.
cues.zh: 我们不再去验证源代码是否安装正确，甚至不再验证源码本身是否正确。我们只检查结果，以及关于该结果的数学证明。所以这是一种黑盒证明，正好提供了你所需要的东西，也就是证明这些密文确实被正确混合了。你关心的也就只有这一点。

cues.en: One subtle case where what you're saying matters is, for example, maybe the random number generator that shuffles these things around is not very good, and it didn't really shuffle them very well. We actually can't test for that. We just know that they were shuffled. We don't know how well they were shuffled. And so we fix that by saying a bunch of people will shuffle them. And we hope that at least one of them will do a good enough job.
cues.zh: 在一种微妙的情况下，你刚才说的确实很重要，比如，负责打乱这些密文的随机数生成器可能不太好，并没有真正打乱得足够彻底。实际上我们无法对此进行检测。我们只能知道它们被打乱了，却不知道打乱的程度如何。因此我们的解决办法是，让一群人轮流来打乱。这样我们就能寄希望于，至少其中有一个人能打乱得足够彻底。

cues.en: But that's the subtle distinction. And it's what I think is particularly cool about this cryptographic verification, which is that you say, I don't care how you write the code. You want to write it in Fortran? Have a blast. Just whatever you want to write, that's fine. It actually even enables proprietary models for voting companies that are very afraid of releasing their source code. I don't think they should be afraid, but they are. So we say, OK, don't release your source code, but produce the mathematical proofs that let us know that you did the right job.
cues.zh: 但这就是微妙的区别所在。而且我认为这种密码学验证特别酷的地方在于，你可以说，我不在乎你用什么方式写代码。你想用 Fortran 写？请便。你想怎么写都行，没问题。它甚至还支持专有模型，适用于那些极度害怕公开源代码的计票公司。虽然我觉得他们没必要害怕，但他们确实怕。所以我们说，行，不用公开源码，但要提供数学证明，让我们知道你们确实做对了，

cues.en: without telling us how you did it. But this is a key question. I'm really glad you asked it. Thank you. Yes. Has this been implemented? It turns out that the company that has implemented this and come the closest to getting it deployed is a company called VoteHere in Seattle. They have had a very hard time getting this approved and used.
cues.zh: 而无需透露具体实现细节。但这是个关键问题。我很高兴你提出来，谢谢。对。这个落实了吗？事实证明，实现这一技术且最接近实际部署的公司，是西雅图一家名为 VoteHere 的公司。他们在推动这一技术的审批和应用上面临了重重阻碍。

cues.en: even though they've made unbelievable advances in the practicality of it, especially in the vote casting sense. It's very difficult to actually show people and explain to people how revolutionary this is. Because if you look at the talk I just gave, and I've given a dozen of these before, it's really hard to explain to people all the interesting details of it without getting too technical. And this is where this stuff gets really hard and sometimes disappointing, which is that it's pretty advanced.
cues.zh: 尽管他们在实用性上已经取得了难以置信的进步，尤其是在投票这个应用场景中。但要真正向人们展示并解释这有多具革命性，仍然非常困难。因为如果你看我刚做的那场演讲——这类演讲我已经做过十几次——就会知道，要想不涉及太多技术细节，就很难向人们解释其中所有有趣的细节。而这就是这类东西真正困难、有时也令人失望的地方：它相当先进。

cues.en: And people believe that because it's advanced, it can't be a good system because a voting system needs to be understandable by everybody and so on and so forth. So that's a very deep and interesting conversation. I've written quite a bit about it. My personal feeling is that if the process is public, if the algorithms are public, there are people who can help you verify it. And as long as it's open, as long as the only thing preventing you from auditing is just skills and reading enough books.
cues.zh: 而人们会觉得，正因为它很先进，它就不可能是好系统，因为投票系统需要让每个人都能理解，诸如此类。所以这是一个非常深入且有趣的讨论。我已经就此写过不少内容。我个人觉得，如果流程是公开的，如果算法是公开的，就会有人能帮你验证它。而且只要它是开放的，只要阻碍你审计的唯一因素只是技能和读足够多的书。

cues.en: then that's a much better system than auditing by privilege, being the right person at the right time who gets to audit. So even though this is more technically complicated and the adoption process is bound to be gruesome, I still think it's better because there's no preference as to who gets to audit. If you want to put in the effort, you can. It's open to you. Are there risks that there are not enough implementers and so that one implementer could corrupt the system? I think the right question or the sort of the question that would
cues.zh: 那这套系统就远好于特权审计，也就是只有在对的时间出现的对的人才能审计。所以即便这在技术上更复杂，推广过程也注定极其痛苦，但我依然认为它更好，因为谁能审计没有任何偏好。只要你愿意付出努力，你就能去审。它向所有人开放。那是否存在实现者不足的风险，以至于某一个实现者就能破坏系统？我认为更切中要害、或者说更贴近问题本质的提问应该是，

cues.en: at a closer problem would be, are there enough verifiers? Because if there's only one implementer, but plenty of verifiers, it's totally fine, right? Well, they should be writing, that's right. So implementers of verification systems, fair enough. Yes, there should be enough implementers of verification systems to make sure that this is done correctly. Is there a risk that there aren't enough?
cues.zh: 验证者足够多吗？因为如果只有一个实现者，但验证者足够多，那就完全没问题，对吧？好吧，他们应该去编写，确实如此。所以应该说是验证系统的实现者，这么说很合理。是的，验证系统需要有足够多的实现者，以确保这一切能正确执行。那是否存在不够多的风险呢？

cues.en: I don't know. I think this would make a very good project for your average grad student or your average, all these folks who want to build useful systems that are of a certain technical level. Great job for Google, too. The point is that anyone with a little bit of extra time could write the code. And if your family only trusts you to help them with technology, you could write the couple hundred lines of code, because really that's all it is, to verify this. And you could say, yes, I've checked it. It went OK.
cues.zh: 我也不确定。我觉得这对普通的准研究生来说会是个非常棒的项目，或者对于那些想要构建达到一定技术水准的实用系统的人来说都很合适。对 Google 来说也是个大展身手的好机会。关键在于，任何有点空闲时间的人都能写出这段代码。如果你的家人只信任你帮他们解决技术问题，你完全可以写出那几百行代码来验证它——因为真的就只需要这么点代码。然后你就可以说，没错，我检查过了，一切正常。

cues.en: That's the real power in my mind. And you can ask anybody with the skills and they can write the verification code. The verification code is much shorter than the proof code, by the way. Yes, another question. It's verification of the results of the output. So it is black box in that sense, but it's not just.
cues.zh: 在我看来，这才是真正的威力所在。你可以去找任何有能力的人，他们都能写出验证代码。顺便提一句，验证代码比证明代码要短得多。好的，请问下一个问题。这是对输出结果的验证。所以从这个角度来看它确实是黑盒的，但又不仅限于此。

cues.en: And the results come with these proofs, right, these interactive proofs I mentioned, where the math tells you it must have been done correctly. cues.zh: 结果会附带这些证明，对吧，就是我提到的这些交互式证明，数学会告诉你它一定是被正确完成的。我知道，对习惯测试、习惯黑盒测试和白盒测试的人来说，这非常奇怪，非常反常。它本来就应该显得很反常。也希望……

cues.en: You know, the only thing I can hope for in this talk is to prompt you to look more into it because all of these cryptographic proofs, these zero-knowledge proofs, are really counterintuitive at first. They really go against the grain of typical software engineering, but they are truly powerful in the sense that you don't need to look at the source code. You just need to look at the output, and the output is self-certifying. Yes, please. Do they get to choose their random numbers in the process?
cues.zh: 你知道，这场演讲里我唯一能期望的，就是促使你再多了解一下，因为所有这些密码学证明、这些零知识证明，一开始都真的很反直觉。它们确实违背典型软件工程的做法，但它们真正强大的地方在于，你不需要看源代码。你只需要看输出，而输出是自证的。是的，请提问。在这个过程中，他们可以自己选择随机数吗？

cues.en: Wow, that's a really deep question, because if you get to choose your random numbers, then you can maybe put some subliminal information in there, and it gets a little crazy. Choosing the right random numbers is an interesting challenge, and there are different ways to do that. That's a whole other conversation, but it's a good question. The hard thing is making sure you're picking good random numbers, but you're not giving individuals in the system too much power that they can start using this as a side channel, basically.
cues.zh: 哇，这个问题真是有深度，因为如果你能自己选择随机数，就可能会在里面夹带隐蔽信息，事情就会变得有点离谱。如何选择合适的随机数是个很有意思的挑战，也有不同的实现方式。这完全是另一个话题了，不过问得很好。难点在于，既要保证选出高质量的随机数，又不能给系统中的个人太大权力，以防他们基本上将其作为侧信道来利用。

cues.en: That's correct. So can the voter and the machine pick random numbers together? That's generally the approach that's taken, getting some randomness from both sides. The problem is making sure you do that without making the process too complicated for voters. That's the difficulty. Yes?
cues.zh: 没错。那么选民和机器能否共同生成随机数呢？通常采用的就是这种方法，即双方各自贡献一部分随机性。问题在于，如何做到这一点的同时，又不会让选民的操作变得过于繁琐。难就难在这里。请讲？

cues.en: Yes, so Barbara Simmons was here you're saying from a couple weeks ago and she's from verified voting and you're saying that's Yeah Right, so you're saying that Barbara Simmons you asked if why don't doesn't verified voting set their sights on systems more like this one Sorry
cues.zh: 是的，你说 Barbara Simmons 几周前来过，她来自 Verified Voting；你说没错，你问 Barbara Simmons，为什么 Verified Voting 不把目标放在更像这样的系统上。抱歉。

cues.en: And she said that's not really their goal. I think to be as objective as I can be about this, there's a number of people who think truly honestly that we are never going to be able to implement these systems, or at least not anytime soon. My personal opinion is that if you look at how far the technology has come, and it's much further along than what I've explained here,
cues.zh: 她说那其实不是他们的目标。我想尽量客观地说，确实有不少人真心认为，我们永远无法实现这些系统，或者至少短期内不行。所以，我们能做的最好就是给现有系统加上纸质记录、提高可审计性，而不去彻底改变它们的工作方式。我个人认为，如果你看看这项技术已经发展到什么程度——它比我这里讲的还要走得远得多，

cues.en: We are really ready to start testing this stuff. And we actually probably have a duty to start testing this stuff, because in the end, I think it's much more democratic to have as many people as possible be able to verify it. But there are honest disagreements about how ready this technology is. And I think Barbara fits in the category of folks who certainly is aware of this technology, but doesn't think it's quite ready. Yes? That's a very good question, which is maybe the readiness is not a technological question. It's a societal acceptance question. I think that's true.
cues.zh: 我们真的已经准备好开始测试这些东西了。而且我们可能也有责任开始测试，因为归根结底，让尽可能多的人能够验证它，会民主得多。但关于这项技术到底有多成熟，确实存在善意的分歧。我认为 Barbara 属于那类人：她当然了解这项技术，但不认为它已经足够成熟。是吧？这是个很好的问题——也许准备程度不是技术问题，而是社会接受度的问题。我认为确实如此。

cues.en: At the same time, the argument has often been made that we don't seem to worry about the acceptability of a lot of other technology that we use for life-saving purposes on a day-to-day basis. What we care about is the auditability process and the involvement of enough people. In the case of voting, we should be able to involve as many people as wish to, but I think it's acceptable to require a certain level of technical knowledge to do so. But, you know, that's a really...
cues.zh: 同时，人们经常提出这样的论点：对于日常用于救生目的的许多其他技术，我们似乎并不担心其可接受性。我们关心的是可审计流程，以及是否有足够多的人参与。就投票而言，我们应该能让所有愿意参与的人都参与进来，但我认为要求参与者具备一定技术水平是可以接受的。不过，你知道，这真的……

cues.en: That's a tough discussion. It's a tough one. Yes. Yes. That's correct. So the question is, what about things that are more than just voting for one candidate? Turns out voting for multiple candidates you can do with homomorphic tallying and you can probably do with mixed net too. But the interesting question there, when you choose to publish individual ballots, is you hit that issue I was talking at the beginning, which is the inherent limitations of a system
cues.zh: 这是一场艰难的讨论。确实很难。是的。是的。没错。所以问题是，不只是给一个候选人投票的情况呢？事实证明，给多个候选人投票可以用同态计票来做，大概也可以用混合网络来做。但有意思的问题是，当你选择公布单张选票时，就会碰到我一开始谈到的那个问题，也就是系统的固有局限

cues.en: when you have a given output. If you give the voter the ability to embed significant information in their ballot, for example, rank the following 25 candidates according to your order of preference, right, then you could just pick the first two you really like and use the bottom 23 to embed information about who you are, right, as a subliminal channel. cues.zh: 在输出给定的情况下。如果你让选民能够在选票中嵌入重要信息，比如按偏好顺序对以下25名候选人排序，那么你就可以只挑出真正喜欢的前两名，用后23名作为一种隐蔽信道，嵌入关于你是谁的信息。所以这里的困难要根本得多。在其他这些投票系统中，如果能在选票中嵌入这么多额外信息，你还能获得多少可验证性？

cues.zh: 是的，问题是，我们能不能先从学生选举做起，让大家逐渐接受这种理念，习惯之后，最终让世界变得更美好。我们当中有些人一直在尝试这种策略，而且在某种程度上还算成功。这里必须称赞一下 David Chow 和他的团队，因为他们已经用过其中一种系统了，也就是 Punchscan。

cues.en: David Chow system, which is also a paper-based system, a bit like Scratch and Vote, but with some slightly different technology. And in fact, it might be counterproductive to go that route. And we really just need to have
cues.zh: David Chow 的系统同样基于纸质媒介，有点像 Scratch & Vote，只是技术上略有不同。他们用纸张、打印机、打孔机以及所需的一切设备把系统落了地，并且已经用它举办了几次学生选举。他们正沿着这条路线探索，也许这条路最终真能成功。但还有另一种观点认为，学生选举永远只会被当作小打小闹的玩具选举，走这条路甚至可能适得其反。我们真正需要的，其实是

cues.en: a method for testing in real elections. And that method might be, you pick a precinct and you say, this year you guys are the guinea pig precinct, and here's how it's going to work. So there are different points of view on this. We've got to wrap up. Folks, thanks so much for.
cues.zh: 一种在真实选举中进行测试的方法。比如，你可以挑选一个选区，并告诉大家，今年你们选区作为试点小白鼠，具体流程是这样的：大家先来用这种新技术投票，要是出了问题，明天再来用旧技术投一次，事情就是这样。所以关于这一点存在不同的看法。我们得收尾了。各位，非常感谢大家。
